source.title: [Replication] Conjecture's Sparse Coding in Small Transformers

record.tranche_reason: The post reports sparse-coding results for learned features in a small transformer, but does not measure whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs or test whether neurons are polysemantic.
record.gate_note: The study analyzes sparse-autoencoder feature dictionaries and their similarity, training-time changes, and sparsity relative to the neuron basis. These are related to feature representation, but the study does not compare neuron responses to unrelated inputs or systematically compare the learned features with the neuron basis for interpretability.
record.test_reason: The post trains sparse autoencoders on MLP activations of a small custom transformer, assuming a superposition framing. It reports only the method's own behaviour: dictionary similarity across sizes, convergence with training, and how dense features are over neurons. It never measures whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs, so it uses the idea as a tool without testing any version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors find that sparse coding recovers consistent features across dictionary sizes with bimodal MCS, that convergence with training is uncertain, and that the diagonal hyperparameter lines were an artefact of the l1 scaling. They also find that learned features are not sparse over neurons, and that interpretability is preliminary and not yet compared with the neuron basis.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains sparse autoencoders on activations from a custom-trained small transformer and compares feature dictionaries; it does not apply a neuron-response polysemanticity measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: Dictionary size changes the pattern of feature matches; additional sparse-autoencoder training raises MMCS slowly. The authors also report that dividing the l1-loss term by dictionary size caused diagonal hyperparameter patterns, and removing that division changed the sweep pattern.

fits_no_version.finding: In layer 2 of a 6-layer, 128-wide-MLP transformer, SAE dictionaries of different sizes share a set of highly similar features (bimodal MCS), alongside many features with no match.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse-autoencoder dictionaries on small-transformer MLP activations consistently recover a subset of features, more numerous than the neurons, across dictionary sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: Further SAE training raises MMCS-with-larger slowly and increases the count of features above 0.9 MCS; convergence is uncertain.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Additional SAE training improves dictionary agreement, with convergence not established.

fits_no_version.finding: Learned features spread over about 83–85 effective neurons out of 128, versus 82 for random vectors (Simpson index).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features in small transformers are not sparse in the neuron basis. This indirectly suggests neurons mix many features, but neuron responses were not measured.

record.problems: The post says dictionary convergence with additional training is uncertain. Interpretability is based on selected maximum-activation examples and was not systematically compared with the neuron basis or other feature-extraction methods. Several reported outcomes have no exact numerical values.
record.rows_left_out: No separate row for the selected maximum-activation examples: the post describes them as apparently interpretable but explicitly says a systematic comparison is still needed, and they do not measure neuron polysemanticity.

untested.parts: Share of language-model MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts; neurons were not examined directly.
Whether neuron polysemanticity is caused by superposition. The post recovers many more SAE features (up to 4096) than the 128 neurons but never links this to neuron responses.
Polysemanticity without capacity pressure; not studied.
Dependence on architecture, activation function or regularization; not studied.
Reinterpretation of canonical polysemantic neurons; not studied.
Measurement dependence of neuron polysemanticity. A neuron-basis interpretability comparison is only planned.

record.verdict_notes: I changed the reader's relation and tranche from discusses/T6 to uses_without_test/T4: this is a replication of an SAE method that reports the method's own performance. The dense-over-neurons result is suggestive for V2/V3, since each feature loads on most neurons. It is not a measure of neuron polysemanticity, so it is recorded only under fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: Neuron responses to multiple unrelated image inputs in vision models.
The share of MLP neurons in language models responding to unrelated tokens or contexts, including variation by layer.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise because the network represents more sparse features than neurons and packs them together.
Polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure from initialization, regularization, or training noise.
How polysemantic neuron prevalence changes with activation function, architecture, or regularization, and its relation to performance.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons have a shared coherent feature or related jobs when examined with better tools.
How measurement range or explanation scoring changes whether neurons count as polysemantic.
